transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-10
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Vega (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Arcadia ML), Tom Reynolds (Arcadia Infra), Dr. Ellen Park (Arcadia CISO)

Summary (auto): Initial discovery for on-prem air-gapped deployment for PHI workloads; focus on offline updates, hardware constraints, and compliance.

[00:00] Carlos: Hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:05] Maya: Yep can hear you, thanks Carlos.
[00:07] Tom: Good here.
[00:10] Carlos: Great. Quick intros, I'm Carlos, AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer. Priya do you want to say hi?
[00:18] Priya: Hi all, Priya Nair, SE focusing on private/on-prem deployments and inference performance.
[00:23] Maya: Maya Singh, Head of ML at Arcadia, we run a bunch of clinical NLP workloads and patient-facing features.
[00:28] Tom: Tom Reynolds, Head of Infrastructure, I'll be owning anything that touches our datacenter and air-gap procedures.
[00:33] Ellen: Dr. Ellen Park, CISO, I'll be focused on compliance, encryption, and offline update controls.
[00:39] Carlos: Awesome thanks. The goal for today is to understand your constraints—air-gap requirements, update cadence, hardware—and then we'll outline how Redwood Private can be deployed in an on-prem air-gapped environment. Sound good?
[00:48] Maya: Yep. For context, our primary drivers are PHI handling, FHIR integrations, and we need an isolated environment with no outbound internet from the inference hosts.
[00:57] Tom: And we have strict change windows and a validated offline update process; we can't have pods pulling from public repos during runtime.
[01:05] Ellen: Also SOC2 and we are pursuing ISO, we need audit trails, HSM-backed keys, SSO with SAML, RBAC, and we need to validate software provenance for any model updates.
[01:15] Priya: Totally understood. Quick high-level: Redwood Private supports a VPC/on-prem control plane with an optional air-gapped installer. Our offline packages include signed artifacts and a documented update process that you run through your secure pipeline. We also support KMS/HSM integrations for key wrapping.
[01:29] Tom: When you say "air-gapped installer" what does that look like? Is it an all-in-one VM image or a set of packages we install behind the firewall?
[01:36] Priya: It's a set of signed binaries and container images we provide via an offline bundle. You can host them on your internal registry. There's a verification step using a signing key. The control plane can be deployed in a separate management network that has limited egress only during initial bootstrap if you choose; or fully air-gapped where all artifacts are scp'ed in.
[01:53] Ellen: How do you handle provenance? We require cryptographic verification and a chain of custody for every model and binary.
[01:58] Priya: We provide SHA256 checksums and signed manifests. For models, we can provide signed model artifacts and a manifest that includes model hashes, training metadata (as available), and a signature that you verify during ingestion. We also integrate with customer HSM for key signing if needed.
[02:14] Maya: What about model updates—our security ops want to approve every patch and model change. Can we control the rollout schedule?
[02:20] Carlos: Yes you can pin model versions, and Redwood's rollout system supports canary and manual approval gates. In private deployments you control the push process; Redwood provides the packaged artifacts and the tooling to apply them.
[02:29] Tom: Performance side: our infra has a mix of A100 and H100 GPUs, limited NVLink topologies, some nodes are single-socket. How does Redwood handle kernel selection and memory/kv cache when you have mixed hardware?
[02:42] Priya: Our runtime detects available hardware and selects optimized kernels accordingly. For mixed clusters we recommend defining node pools by GPU type—dedicated pools for H100 vs A100—so the runtime routes requests appropriately. For KV cache and batching, we expose config controls; we also ship heuristics to avoid cross-node KV dependencies unless you have a shared NVLink fabric.
[03:02] Maya: So for low-latency 1-3 token generation vs long context multi-turn clinical summarization, can we tune different routes?
[03:09] Priya: Yes you can have per-route model and performance policies. Low-latency routes can be pinned to smaller context models on H100 pools with aggressive batching disabled, while long-context routes go to nodes sized for memory with larger KV cache.
[03:21] Tom: What's the offline update frequency? Are we expected to pull weekly security patches? We have quarterly change windows ideally.
[03:27] Carlos: We can accommodate quarterly or ad-hoc update cadences. The offline bundle is versioned, so you can choose which bundle to apply. Security patches we recommend applying promptly, but we support backport notes and critical fixes with documented risk.
[03:39] Ellen: About keys—our policy requires keys to never leave the HSM and to perform server-side decryption within a validated module. Does Redwood support HSM-backed model encryption and KMS wrapping?
[03:50] Priya: Yes, Redwood supports customer-managed HSM/KMS. We can integrate with PKCS#11-compatible HSMs. Keys used for model encryption remain in your HSM; Redwood's runtime is configured to decrypt using the HSM interface at load time. We also support envelope encryption for model blobs.
[04:07] Maya: Great. On telemetry and observability, we need logs but with PHI redaction and the ability to keep logs entirely on-prem with retention policies.
[04:15] Priya: You can ship logs to your internal ELK/Splunk stack; Redwood's default traces and metrics can be disabled or routed only to your self-hosted endpoints. We also support token-level cost estimations but that can run locally.
[04:28] Tom: Network-wise, is there any requirement for outbound connections after install? We want zero egress.
[04:33] Carlos: For fully air-gapped installations, no outbound connection is required. Certain features (like automatic model catalog updates) require egress; those are optional and can be disabled.
[04:42] Maya: Can you walk through a typical POC for a company like ours? We want to test a small set of endpoints with real PHI redaction and a simulated patient portal traffic profile.
[04:51] Priya: Sure. Typical POC: we provide an offline bundle and deploy a pilot cluster with 2-4 nodes. We onboard a model (either an open model or your vetted model) and run a workload generator to mimic your traffic. We measure latency, throughput, and cost per token. We'll also validate the update path — how you ingest a new signed model artifact.
[05:10] Tom: How long does that take? We have a 6-week window to prove throughput and reliability.
[05:14] Carlos: A pilot typically runs 3-6 weeks. The first week is install and baseline tests, then two weeks of workload testing and tuning, and a final week for security/ops validation. That fits within 6 weeks.
[05:24] Ellen: On auditability, do you provide an append-only audit log with tamper evidence?
[05:29] Priya: We provide audit logs that can be shipped to your SIEM. For tamper-evidence, we can integrate with your secure logging solution, and produce signed log manifests on rotation. Full chain-of-custody can be supported with HSM-signed checkpoints.
[05:44] Maya: Cost — we are trying to compare hosted vs private. Can you give a ballpark for a dedicated on-prem license model? We have around 12M tokens/day in peak in our estimates.
[05:55] Carlos: We'll provide a formal pricing doc, but generally private deployments have a platform fee plus node licensing or support tiers. For planning, our team will size GPU counts and estimate infrastructure opex; we can run an internal model to give you cost-per-token estimates for both hosted and private.
[06:09] Tom: For mixed nodes, if we have a few H100s and a couple older A40s, will Redwood degrade gracefully or is there strict compatibility?
[06:18] Priya: The runtime will detect and advertise capabilities. It's best to isolate legacy hardware into separate pools so that high-memory workloads aren't scheduled on undersized GPUs. We also have model variants and quantization profiles that can be deployed for older GPUs.
[06:30] Ellen: Any third-party penetration tests or security certifications we should be aware of?
[06:35] Carlos: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and we can share our security pack. For private deployments, customers often run their own pen tests; we coordinate and provide guidance and support.
[06:45] Maya: One more on licensing — can trained customer models remain entirely under our control? We don't want model artifacts uploaded to a Redwood-hosted catalog.
[06:53] Priya: Absolutely. In private deployments you control model storage. Redwood can run with local-only model stores and won't push models to any Redwood-hosted catalog unless you opt in.
[07:02] Tom: About the installer—what are system-level dependencies? OS versions, container runtime—our infra team needs specifics.
[07:09] Priya: We support mainstream Linux distros (RHEL, Ubuntu), container runtimes like containerd and Docker (enterprise), and orchestration via K8s. For fully air-gapped setups we supply offline CRI images, Helm charts, and a documented install script. We'll send a detailed compatibility matrix.
[07:25] Ellen: For logging and monitoring of access to PHI, do you keep query-level content in logs by default?
[07:31] Priya: By default, logs include metadata and anonymized traces; we can turn off or redact request payloads. For compliance, customers often configure full redaction or route payload logs to a secured vault.
[07:44] Maya: On a technical note—does Redwood runtime rely on any cloud provider-specific SDKs requiring outbound keys? We can't have cloud keys present on the nodes.
[07:54] Priya: No, the private runtime is cloud-agnostic. Any cloud provider integrations are optional and not required for core inference. No outbound keys must be present unless you enable integrations.
[08:02] Tom: For GPU drivers and NCCL versions—do you require specific versions for H100/H100X?
[08:09] Priya: We provide a recommended driver and CUDA/NCCL matrix. For H100 we recommend CUDA 12.x and compatible NCCL; we'll include that in the compatibility matrix and can validate drivers during the pilot.
[08:22] Maya: Is model quantization supported in the private runtime? We sometimes prefer int8 for throughput.
[08:27] Priya: Yes, quantization is supported. We also provide model-specific quantization profiles and advice; some quantization paths are GPU-specific. We'll share recommended quantization/perf tradeoffs per model.
[08:38] Carlos: I want to make sure we're capturing success criteria — Maya, what would make this a successful POC?
[08:44] Maya: Low-latency patient query responses under 200ms P95 for short routing, reliable long-context summarization under 2s P95 when batched. Also, security approval for the offline update process and demonstration of RBAC and audit logs.
[08:58] Ellen: Plus evidence of key management and that model artifacts never leave our network.
[09:03] Priya: Got it. We'll map those to test cases.
[09:06] Tom: Any standard attack surface we should be worried about? For example, model weights exfil?
[09:11] Priya: Typical controls: network segmentation, encryption at rest and in transit, strict IAM, and host-level monitoring. For extra assurance, we can run a code-level review and provide a read-only model serving mode if you want to prevent writes to model stores.
[09:26] Maya: For the POC we'll probably use a smaller LLM — do you have curated small models for clinical domain or do we bring our own fine-tuned models?
[09:35] Carlos: We have a model catalog with curated open models; for clinical domain often customers bring their fine-tuned models. Both approaches are supported.
[09:42] Tom: Is there any telemetry that gets sent back to Redwood in private installs by default?
[09:47] Priya: No telemetry is sent by default in fully air-gapped installs. We only enable telemetry if you opt in, and even then telemetry can be limited to anonymized metrics and sent via customer-controlled endpoints.
[09:58] Maya: Regarding SLAs, what can Redwood commit to on private installs?
[10:03] Carlos: For private deployments we offer enterprise support tiers with SLA-backed response times and optional on-call support. Exact SLA terms are part of the enterprise contract.
[10:12] Tom: In the case of hardware failure, do you provide node replacement guidance?
[10:17] Priya: Yes, we document recovery steps and we can provide runbooks. For critical nodes, we can help configure high-availability and failover patterns.
[10:25] Ellen: For regulatory requirements like data localization, if we need a completely offline pipeline for model retraining, does Redwood facilitate offline training artifacts transfer?
[10:35] Priya: Redwood focuses on inference; for training artifacts we can support workflows where artifacts are exported and validated offline. We provide guidance but don't run training in your environment unless engaged separately.
[10:46] Maya: One last question on licensing: can the platform be installed on-prem under a subscription or is it a perpetual license?
[10:52] Carlos: Both are possible; common is a subscription plus a support contract. We'll detail options in our pricing doc.
[10:59] Tom: Okay great, that answers a lot. Next steps again?
[11:03] Carlos: We'll send the security pack and compatibility matrix. Priya will follow up on hardware sizing and schedule a deeper tech call. Maya to share token estimates and sample workloads. Ellen will share compliance checklist items.
[11:16] Maya: I'll send over the workload spreadsheet and example logs.
[11:20] Ellen: I'll send a short compliance list and our change window policy.
[11:24] Tom: I'll coordinate on available nodes and driver inventory.
[11:28] Carlos: Perfect. Anything else before we wrap?
[11:31] Maya: No, that's good.
[11:33] Carlos: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and schedule the sizing call.
[11:37] Priya: Thanks all.
[11:39] Ellen: Thanks.
[11:41] End of call.
